welcome_lead: Pick the right algorithm for the job and justify your choice.
meta_desc: GCSE Computer Science stretch adventure on choosing between searches and sorts with reasoning.
final_note: You can defend your algorithm choice with confidence.

concepts.def: Gaining one benefit costs something else.
Work needed before an algorithm can run.
Equal items keep their original order.
Sort defined by calling itself, e.g. merge sort.
Trade between speed and memory used.

walkthroughs.body_html: Binary search needs a sorted list (setup cost ~O(n log n)). If you only search once, linear search might win overall. Sort once, query many times → binary search dominates.
Bubble and insertion sort sort 'in place' — no extra arrays. Merge sort needs extra memory to hold halves. If memory is tight on an embedded system, in-place sorts win.

State the size, whether the list is sorted, and any memory constraints. Then pick the algorithm and justify with complexity. Example: 'List is huge and unsorted → merge sort because O(n log n) beats O(n^2).'
